name: Idakho-Isukha-Tiriki
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.source_named: Ebarb, Kristopher 2014. Tone and Variation in Idakho and Other Luhya Varieties. PhD diss., Indiana University (556pp)
earlier_scan.note: Tonal Bantu; large phonology diss. plausibly notes stress/penult prominence; not openly fetchable

sources.citation: Nandama, Sussy K. 2022. A Study of the Tone System of Lwisukha Nouns. MA thesis, University of Nairobi (hdl 11295/162079), xx+352 pp.
sources.note: Ch.2 (p.28) lists 'tone, intonation, stress, vowel length and pitch among others' as Lwisukha suprasegments but states only tone is treated; p.1 mentions 'tone and stress' as possible dialect-classification criteria. No statement of where stress falls. Body: Lwisukha has H, L, downstepped H and toneless syllables; 39 noun tone patterns in isolation; HTA and H-tone-insertion rules.

sources.citation: Masolia, Everlyn K. 2018. A Lexical and Phonological Variation in Logooli, Lutirichi and Lumundu: a Sociolinguistics Variationist Approach. MA thesis, University of Nairobi (hdl 11295/104673), xvi+88 pp.
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: not located online or at Harvard
sources.note: Segmental/lexical variables only; no tone or stress description.

sources.citation: Paster, Mary & Yuni Kim. 2011. Downstep in Tiriki. Linguistic Discovery 9(1): 71-104. doi:10.1349/PS1.1537-0852.A.390
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: open copy online (also: harvard online access (harvardkey))
sources.note: Nothing. Sec.3.1 'Basics of Tiriki tonology' (p.78): TBU is the mora; underlying three-way contrast H / toneless / L reducing to surface H vs L (+downstepped H); Meeussen's Rule, H Tone Anticipation, default L insertion. The words stress/accent occur only for diacritics; no statement on word stress or penultimate prominence anywhere in the 34 pp.

sources.citation: Nandama, S. & Oduor, J. A. N. 2022. The High Tone Anticipation Rule in the Lwisukha Dialect of Luyia. (UoN repository hdl 11295/160312), 16 pp.
sources.note: Tone rule (HTA) only; no mention of stress.

sources.citation: Nandama, Sussy & Jane A. N. Oduor. 2020. The Tonal Patterns of Nouns in Isolation in the Lwisukha Dialect of Luyia. (UoN repository hdl 11295/153500), 23 pp.
sources.note: Tone patterns of nouns only; no mention of stress.

sources.citation: Osotsi, Eric M. 2020. A Systematic Reconstruction of the Phonology of Proto-Luyia: A Comparative Analysis. University of Nairobi thesis (hdl 11295/154048), 127 pp.
sources.note: Segmental reconstruction across Luyia dialects incl. Lwitakho/Lwisukha/Lutiriki; no suprasegmental section, nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Shidiavai, Morand S. 2015. A Phonological Analysis of Lwidakho Loanwords from Kiswahili and English. MA thesis, University of Nairobi (hdl 11295/94315).
sources.note: Segmental and syllable-structure adaptation in OT; pp.4-5 state suprasegmental changes 'fall beyond the scope of this study'; p.83 notes Lwidakho is tonal. Nothing on stress placement.

sources.citation: Hyman, Larry M. 2013. Penultimate lengthening in Bantu. (on file from another language's audit)
sources.note: Second-hand survey: Tiriki JE413 is listed in Appendix 3 'Languages with positionally restricted vowel length', not among penultimate-lengthening languages; no stress statement for Luyia.

sources.citation: Botne, Robert. 2009 [issued 2011]. The curious case of auxiliary -many'a in Lwitaxo. Studies in African Linguistics 38(2): 93-112.
sources.note: Morphosyntax; fn.1 only says tone is marked where possible and occasionally differentiates lexical items. Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Yukawa, Yasutoshi (湯川恭敏). 2003. イスハ語動詞アクセント試論 [A tentative tonal analysis of Isukha verbs]. 36 pp. (in Japanese; CORE 483804192)
sources.note: Yukawa's 'アクセント' = H/L tone marking on vowels; paradigm-by-paradigm tonal analysis of Isukha verb forms (A-type/B-type stems). Text layer is badly garbled scanned; no stress (強勢) statement seen.

sources.citation: Kebeya, Hilda Udali. 1997. Investigating linguistic accommodation between two Luyia dialects: Logooli and Lwitakho. MA thesis, Kenyatta University (hdl 123456789/4124).
sources.note: Ch.4 phonology of Logooli and Lwitakho is consonant-focused and states 'we shall not deal with suprasegmental elements'. Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Ingonga, Lilian Indira. 1991. A comparative study of Ekegusii, Lulogooli and Lwitakho: the phonological, lexical and morphosyntactic structures. MA thesis, Kenyatta University (hdl 123456789/4639).
sources.note: Read via the repository's scanned text bitstream (46 MB scan not downloaded). Lwitakho sketch (pp.33-39): consonant/vowel inventory, CV syllables, phonemic vowel length; no mention of tone or stress at all.

sources.citation: Ebarb, Kristopher J. 2014. Tone and Variation in Idakho and Other Luhya Varieties. PhD dissertation, Indiana University, Bloomington. 556 pp.
